title: Agent Lab: build AI agents from scratch

lessons.title: What a model sees
lessons.summary: an agent is a model in a loop with tools; first, the one flat string a chat model actually reads

sections.html:
You know how a model is trained and how it generates tokens. An agent adds remarkably little on top: a program (the harness) that

  1. sends the model a conversation plus a list of tools it may use,
  2. reads the reply: either a final answer, or a request to call some tools,
  3. runs those tools, appends the results to the conversation, and goes back to step 1.

Claude Code, Cursor's agent, OpenAI's Codex and Deep Research are all this loop, with better tools, better context management, planning, and humans in the right places. This course builds each of those pieces, one lab at a time, until lab 14 is a small coding agent.

There are no messages, only text

A chat API takes a list of messages and a list of tools. The model never sees either. The server runs a chat template (a Jinja program shipped in the model's tokenizer_config.json) that flattens everything into one string with special tokens, and the model simply continues that string. This is the ChatML template used by Qwen 2.5 and Hermes models:

<|im_start|>system
You are a helpful agent.

# Tools
...
<tools>
{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "lookup", "description": "...", "parameters": {...}}}
</tools>
For each function call, return a json object ... within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
How much HBM do 8 H100s have in total?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
<tool_call>
{"name": "lookup", "arguments": {"topic": "H100"}}
</tool_call><|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
<tool_response>
NVIDIA H100 SXM: 80 GB HBM3, ...
</tool_response><|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

Four things to notice, because the rest of the course depends on them:

  • Tools are text in the system prompt. Every tool's JSON schema is pasted in, on every request. Tool definitions cost prompt tokens and attention, which is why tool count and description quality matter (lessons 03 and 04).
  • A tool call is text the model was trained to write. Post-training (SFT and RL on agent trajectories, lesson 13) teaches the model to emit <tool_call>{json}</tool_call> when a tool would help. The server parses it back out into tool_calls. If the model writes slightly broken JSON, parsing fails (lesson 01).
  • Tool results come back as a user turn. In Qwen's template, results are wrapped in <tool_response> inside a user message. Other families differ (Llama 3 uses an ipython role, gpt-oss uses its "harmony" format with channels), but every one of them is a convention learned in training. Use the template the model was trained with, or it gets noticeably worse.
  • **The prompt ends with <|im_start|>assistant\n**, the generation prompt. The model's next tokens are its turn, and it ends the turn by producing <|im_end|>, which the server treats as a stop token.

The number on each step is the size of the prompt, in tokens, once that piece is in it. 373 of the 458 tokens are there before the user has said a word.

The course's model

Every lab runs offline against a mock model: a small Python policy that receives exactly what a real model receives (messages and tool schemas) and returns what a real model would (text or tool calls). That makes every number in the course reproducible on a laptop, and the mock is honest: if your harness forgets to send a tool result back, the mock can't see it either and gets stuck, exactly like a real model.

Every lab also takes --model to run against a real server, so you can compare:

python tools/check_env.py                       # what can this machine reach?
python labs/02_agent_loop/run.py --model ollama:qwen2.5:7b
python labs/02_agent_loop/run.py --model vllm:Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct    # vllm serve ... on :8000
AGENTLAB_BASE_URL=http://gpu-box:30000/v1 python labs/02_agent_loop/run.py --model sglang:Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

The library in agentlab/ is small and readable: llm.py (mock and OpenAI-compatible clients), tools.py (schemas from Python functions), loop.py (the agent loop, which you will write yourself in lab 02), tokens.py (an approximate tokenizer).

Open labs/00_first_call/agent.py and fill in render_chat(messages, tools), following its five TODOs:

  1. The system message; if tools are given, append the # Tools block with one JSON schema per line inside <tools></tools>, and the instruction to answer in <tool_call> tags.
  2. User messages as they are.
  3. Assistant messages: the content (if any), then one <tool_call> {"name": ..., "arguments": {...}} </tool_call> block per call. Note that arguments arrives as a JSON string in OpenAI format; decode it, then re-encode with the template's spacing.
  4. Tool messages: consecutive results go into one user turn, each as <tool_response> ... </tool_response>.
  5. End with the generation prompt.

python labs/00_first_call/run.py             # your agent.py
python labs/00_first_call/run.py --solution  # the reference

It checks your rendering against the reference on 6 conversations, prints the full prompt, and counts tokens.

79% of the prompt is tool definitions. Two short tools cost 364 tokens and a whole four-message conversation costs 458. Real agents ship 20 to 100 tools, and Claude Code's system prompt plus tools is well over 10,000 tokens. That cost is paid on every request, which is why prefix caching (lesson 13) matters so much for agents: the tools and system prompt are identical across steps, so a server can reuse their KV cache.

Nine special tokens carry all the structure. <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are single tokens in the vocabulary, which plain text can't produce by accident. (Whether a user can inject them by typing the string depends on the tokenizer settings, a real security concern.) <tool_call> and <tool_response> are added tokens in Qwen 2.5 too, so the model learns sharp boundaries for calls and results.

Our token counts are estimates. agentlab/tokens.py approximates a BPE tokenizer with a regex. With --model, servers report the true prompt_tokens, which typically differs by 10 to 30%. The ratios are what to take away.

lessons.title: Tool calling from scratch
lessons.summary: JSON schemas from Python functions, parsing the messy calls real models write, validating arguments

sections.html:
Three pieces of code sit between a model and your functions. Servers like vLLM and Ollama run some of them for you (their "tool parsers"), but they fail in production often enough that you should know exactly what they do.

1. Describe the function: JSON schema

The model can only call what it has read about. A tool definition is a name, a description, and a JSON schema for the arguments:

def book_gpu(gpu: Literal["H100", "A100", "B200"], hours: int, tags: Optional[List[str]] = None):
    """Reserve GPUs.

    Args:
        gpu: which GPU type
        hours: how long, in whole hours
    """
{"type": "object",
 "properties": {"gpu":   {"type": "string", "enum": ["H100", "A100", "B200"], "description": "which GPU type"},
                "hours": {"type": "integer", "description": "how long, in whole hours"},
                "tags":  {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "default": null}},
 "required": ["gpu", "hours"]}

Every framework (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, Pydantic AI, smolagents, MCP servers) generates this from type hints and docstrings, as agentlab/tools.py does. The enum matters more than it looks: it is the difference between the model writing "h100", "H-100" or "H100 SXM" and writing a value your code accepts.

2. Parse what the model wrote

When a server has no tool parser for your model, or the model drifts from its format, you get the raw text. Real outputs include:

  • the trained format: <tool_call>{"name": ..., "arguments": {...}}</tool_call>, possibly several in a row (parallel calls);
  • a markdown fence around the JSON, or a sentence of prose before it;
  • Llama 3's <|python_tag|> and its "parameters" key instead of "arguments";
  • arguments as a JSON-encoded string (OpenAI's wire format, which models sometimes imitate);
  • trailing commas, Python-style single quotes;
  • output cut off by max_tokens in the middle of the JSON;
  • braces inside string values ("topic": "kv cache {per token}") that break naive brace matching.

json.loads(text) handles exactly one of those. A robust parser scans for top-level {...} objects while tracking whether it is inside a string, tries strict JSON, then a lenient repair, and reports why it failed (an unterminated object usually means truncation, which is worth telling the model or raising max_tokens).

3. Validate before you run

A parsed call can still be wrong: a missing required argument, "hours": "four", a GPU that isn't in the enum, an argument that doesn't exist, or true for an integer (in Python bool is a subclass of int, a classic bug). Validation turns these into specific messages the model can act on, instead of a stack trace or, worse, a wrong action.

The alternative to parsing and validating is constrained decoding: vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and OpenAI's strict mode can compile the JSON schema into a grammar and mask the logits at every step so invalid output is impossible. It is the right default for production, but it doesn't remove the need for semantic validation (the job id must exist), and grammars can slightly hurt quality when they force tokens the model would not have chosen.

steps.text: <tool_call>{"name": "lookup", "arguments": {"topic": "H100"}}</tool_call>
Sure! I'll check that. {"name": "lookup", "arguments": {"topic": "B200"}}
<|python_tag|>{"name": "calculator", "parameters": {"expression": "7*6"}}
{'name': 'lookup', 'arguments': {'topic': 'H100'},}
<tool_call>{"name": "lookup", "arguments": {"topic": "kv cache
all but the last parse; the last is reported as "unterminated JSON object (was the output truncated?)"

In labs/01_tool_calling/agent.py:

  1. function_schema(fn): walk inspect.signature(fn).parameters with typing.get_type_hints(fn). Map str/int/float/bool to JSON types, List[X] to an array with items, Literal[...] to an enum, Optional[X] to the schema of X. Take descriptions from the docstring's Args: section. Parameters without defaults are required.
  2. parse_tool_calls(text): find top-level JSON objects by counting braces (quotes only count inside an object, so an apostrophe in prose doesn't start a "string"); parse with json.loads, then without trailing commas, then ast.literal_eval; accept arguments or parameters, decode string arguments; return (calls, error).
  3. validate(args, schema): required, unknown, type (bool is not an integer) and enum checks, as human-readable strings.

python labs/01_tool_calling/run.py --solution

fields.label: bad argument sets caught by validate

sections.html:
Only 1 of 12 real-world outputs is pure JSON. Everything else has tags, prose, fences, a different key, or small syntax slips. Servers' built-in parsers handle the format the model was trained on (Hermes tags for Qwen, <|python_tag|> for Llama), and fail when the model deviates. When they fail, the call is usually silently dropped and the text is returned as if it were a final answer, and the agent "finishes" without doing anything. Knowing this failure mode saves hours of debugging.

The truncation case must be an error, not an empty list. If the parser returned [] for a cut-off call, the loop would treat the half-written call as the model's final answer. Returning a reason ("unterminated JSON object, was the output truncated?") lets the harness retry with a larger max_tokens.

Validation's messages are written for the model. "hours should be integer, got str 'four'" is enough for any decent model to fix its next call. Lesson 03 takes this further: error messages are part of the tool's interface.

lessons.title: The agent loop
lessons.summary: ReAct in fifteen lines; parallel calls, bounded steps, errors as observations, and why cost grows with every step

sections.html:
Here is the whole idea. Every agent you have heard of is a variant of this:

messages = [system, user_task]
for step in range(max_steps):
    reply = llm.chat(messages, tools)          # think, maybe ask for tools
    messages.append(reply.message())
    if not reply.tool_calls:
        return reply.text                      # the model decided it is done
    for call in reply.tool_calls:              # act
        result = execute(call)                 # never raises
        messages.append(tool_message(call, result))   # observe
return "stopped: out of steps"

This is ReAct (Yao et al., 2022, "Reason + Act"): the model interleaves reasoning, actions and observations, and each observation shapes the next step. The original paper used text like Thought: … Action: … Observation: …. Today the model's reasoning goes in its content (or a hidden reasoning channel for o-series, gpt-oss, Claude's extended thinking), and actions are structured tool calls, but the loop is the same.

Four rules the harness must enforce

  1. The model decides when to stop, by replying without tool calls. The harness never guesses.
  2. Bound the loop. Models get stuck: they repeat a call, or keep "checking" forever. max_steps is the minimum; production agents also cap tokens, wall time and cost.
  3. Errors are observations, not exceptions. A tool that raises must not crash the agent. Return "Error: ValueError: cannot parse '8 x 80': use numbers and + - * /…" as the tool result, and the model, which can read, fixes its call. Most "the agent is dumb" bugs are harnesses that swallow or hide errors.
  4. Every call gets a result, in order, matched by tool_call_id. APIs reject an assistant message with tool calls that are not all answered, and models trained on well-formed histories get confused by gaps.

Parallel calls

Models can ask for several independent calls in one reply. Here it looks up the H100 and the A100 at once. It saves a model round trip (one prefill and decode) per call, and a harness can run them concurrently. Models were trained to do this, and the system prompt can encourage it ("call several at once when they are independent").

sections.html:
Why agents are expensive

Look at the prompt sizes on that trace: 334, 426, 451 tokens. Every step re-sends the entire history. The prompt grows by each step's output plus each tool's result, so total prompt tokens grow roughly quadratically with the number of steps. A 50-step coding session where tools return file contents can easily send millions of prompt tokens. Two things keep this affordable: prefix caching on the server (lesson 13) and context management in the harness (lesson 04).

In labs/02_agent_loop/agent.py:

  1. execute(box, call): unknown tool → an error string that lists the available tools; otherwise tool.fn(**call.args); any exception → "Error: <Type>: <message>".
  2. run_agent(...): the loop above. Count steps (model calls) and tool_calls, call on_event after each reply and each tool result (that's how --trace prints), and return a Run with stopped="answer" or "max_steps".

python labs/02_agent_loop/run.py --trace
python labs/02_agent_loop/run.py --solution --trace

Three scenarios: a competent model, a runaway model that repeats itself, and a sloppy one that writes 8 x 80 to the calculator.

sections.html:
Three model calls, three tool calls, 1,211 prompt tokens for a 30-token answer. The answer is tiny; the cost is the history re-sent three times, and most of each prompt is the two tool schemas (lesson 00). That ratio only gets worse as tasks get longer.

The runaway is stopped by the harness, not the model. The runaway policy repeats lookup("H100") forever; max_steps=6 ends it with stopped="max_steps". Real models loop like this when a tool keeps returning something they don't expect. Production harnesses also detect repeated identical calls and inject a nudge ("you have called this 3 times with the same arguments").

The error message did the recovering. The calculator raised ValueError with a hint ("use * for multiplication"), the harness returned it as the tool result, and the next call was 8 * 80. If execute had raised instead, the run would have crashed; if it had returned only "error", the model would have had to guess.

lessons.title: Designing tools for models
lessons.summary: the agent-computer interface; names and descriptions pick the tool, errors that teach, arguments that can't be wrong

sections.html:
Anthropic's engineers reported that while building their SWE-bench agent they spent more time on the tools than on the prompt. The SWE-agent paper (Yang et al., 2024) gave it a name: the agent-computer interface (ACI). Tools are a user interface whose user is a model, and that user reads everything literally, has no other documentation, and can't ask you what you meant.

Names and descriptions choose the tool

The model chooses a tool by reading its name and description against the task. Compare:

vaguedescriptive
query(q): "Run a query."get_job_status(job_id): "Status, GPU count, current step and last log line of one training job. Use for 'is job-X running', 'what step'."
do(action, target)scale_deployment(name, replicas): "Set the number of replicas of a serving deployment."
info(x)get_service_metrics(service, window_minutes): "p50/p99 latency, error rate and QPS of a service."

Good descriptions say what the tool returns, when to use it (and when not to), and the format of inputs (job ids look like job-123). Write them like documentation for a smart new colleague. Then test them: watch which tool a real model picks for twenty realistic requests.

Errors that teach

A tool's error message is the only feedback the model gets. Compare what the model sees after asking for job-12, which doesn't exist:

  • KeyError: 'job-12'
  • Error: no job 'job-12'. Did you mean: job-123, job-121? Valid job ids: job-7, job-88, job-121, job-123.

With the first, the model apologizes or guesses. With the second, it retries job-123, and if that isn't what the user meant, it can say so. "Did you mean" with difflib.get_close_matches is ten lines of code and fixes a whole class of failures.

Poka-yoke: make mistakes impossible

Poka-yoke is the manufacturing term for designing a part so it can't be assembled wrong. For tools:

  • Coerce obviously-intended types: "3" → 3 for an integer, "true" → True. Models send numbers as strings surprisingly often.
  • Prefer enums to free strings, and absolute paths to relative ones (Anthropic's SWE-bench agent made path mistakes after moving out of the root directory until its tools required absolute paths).
  • Return less, but what matters: a search that returns 200 lines buries the answer; return the top 10 with a count of the rest.
  • Merge tools that are always called together, and split tools that do two unrelated things. Fewer, sharper tools beat many overlapping ones.

fields.label: string numbers that worked first try with coercion

sections.html:
Tool choice went from 3/12 to 12/12 without changing the model. The lab's "model" just matches words between the task and each tool's name and description, and a real model's attention does a far better version of the same thing. With five tools called query, do, info… it has nothing to match, so it defaults to one. Descriptive names and "use this for…" sentences give it the words to match. Real models are better at guessing than this one, but the direction of the effect is the same, and it grows with the number of tools.

Recovery went from 0/4 to 4/4 with the same tools. Only the error text changed. This is the cheapest reliability improvement in agent engineering. Audit every error your tools can return and ask: could a model fix its call from this message alone?

Coercion turned 0/3 into 3/3 first-try successes. Without it each "3" costs a failed call, an error, and a retry: an extra model round trip and more context. Being liberal in what you accept is a good idea only when the intent is unambiguous; never coerce "delete everything" into anything.

lessons.title: Context engineering and memory
lessons.summary: the context window is working memory; clip tool output, compact old turns, and never drop facts blindly

sections.html:
A model's context window is its only working memory during a run. Everything it knows about the task, its progress and the world is in the prompt, and every tool result makes the prompt bigger. Long agent runs fail in three ways:

  • Cost and latency. Prefill scales with prompt length, and every step re-reads it all (lesson 02).
  • Overflow. The run hits the context limit and the API rejects the request.
  • Context rot. Well before the limit, quality drops: models attend less reliably to facts buried in the middle of a long context ("lost in the middle", Liu et al. 2023; Chroma's 2025 "context rot" study measured the same across frontier models). A 200K-token context is not 200K tokens of reliable memory.

Context engineering is the harness deciding, at every step, what goes into that window. Three techniques cover most of it.

1. Clip tool output at the source

A 700-token log file where one line matters should not cost 700 tokens for the rest of the run. Clip each result: keep the head and tail (structure and the latest state) plus every line matching what matters (ERROR|Traceback|FAILED), and mark the gaps: [... 14 lines elided ...]. Claude Code and Cursor truncate long command output the same way, and good tools take max_results / line-range arguments so the model can ask for more.

2. Compact the middle

When the history passes a budget, replace the old middle with a summary written by the model itself, and keep the system prompt, the task, and the most recent turns verbatim:

[system] [task] [Summary of earlier work: files read so far, every ERROR line, what's next] [last 6 messages]

This is what Claude Code's /compact and auto-compaction do, and what Codex does when its context fills. Two details decide whether it works:

  • The summary prompt must say what to keep. "Summarize the conversation" loses exactly the facts you need. Say "keep the full file list, which files were read, and every ERROR line verbatim".
  • Never split a tool call from its result. The kept tail can't start with a tool message whose assistant call was summarized away. APIs reject that history, and models misread it.

3. Don't just drop the oldest turns

The obvious fix, deleting the oldest messages until it fits, is what many chat apps do. For an agent it is a disaster: the oldest turns hold the plan and the list of work, so the agent forgets what it has done and starts over.

Memory beyond one run

The same ideas extend across runs. Scratchpads and notes: the agent writes progress to a file (NOTES.md, a todo list) and reads it back, so state survives compaction. Long-term memory: facts stored outside the model (Cursor's memories, ChatGPT memory, a vector store) and retrieved into the prompt when relevant. Just-in-time context: rather than pre-loading everything, give the agent tools (grep, read_file with line ranges) to pull in what it needs. Coding agents moved from embedding-based retrieval to agentic search with grep for exactly this reason.

In labs/04_context_memory/agent.py:

python labs/04_context_memory/run.py --solution
python labs/04_context_memory/run.py --solution --trace     # watch the context size per step

Four strategies on the same task: keep everything, drop the oldest turns, clip tool output, clip plus compact.

Keeping everything works here, at 6x the cost. 163K prompt tokens for one task, a 15K peak, and the peak grows with every file. With 200 files it would overflow any context, and long before that the errors in the middle of files would start being missed by a real model.

Dropping the oldest turns found 0 of 5 errors and never finished. It deleted the file list and the early reads, so the agent re-listed the files and started over, again and again, until it hit 40 steps. Forgetting is not neutral: it destroys the plan.

Clip + compact: 9x smaller peak, 6x fewer tokens, all 5 errors. Clipping alone cut the peak to 3.5K because the ERROR lines survive and the INFO noise doesn't. Compaction bounded it at 1.6K: the summary keeps the file list, the progress and every error verbatim, and costs three extra model calls (25 versus 22). That trade, a few summarizer calls for a bounded context, is how every long-running agent works.

What the summary prompt keeps is the whole game. Try weakening it (drop "every ERROR line verbatim" from summarize in run.py) and the agent finishes confidently with errors missing. Compaction failures are silent.

lessons.title: Workflows before agents
lessons.summary: routing, parallel fan-out and evaluator-optimizer; when your code should decide the steps instead of the model

sections.html:
Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (2024) draws a line that is worth keeping in your head for the rest of the course:

  • Workflows: LLM calls orchestrated by your code along predefined paths.
  • Agents: the model directs its own process and tool use, deciding the steps as it goes.

Agents are more flexible, and they cost that flexibility in tokens, latency and predictability. Every step is a decision the model can get wrong. When you know the steps in advance, a workflow is cheaper, faster, easier to test, and usually more accurate. Start with the simplest thing that works: a single well-prompted call, then a workflow, and only then an agent.

The patterns

  • Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence (outline → draft → translate), with code checks between steps.
  • Routing: classify the input, then send it to a specialized prompt (or a cheaper model for easy cases). Each specialist prompt can be optimized without hurting the others.
  • Parallelization: sectioning (independent subtasks at once) or voting (the same task several times, then aggregate). Independent LLM calls are I/O-bound, so a thread pool gives near-linear speedups.
  • Orchestrator-workers: a model breaks the task into subtasks dynamically and delegates them (lesson 09).
  • Evaluator-optimizer: one call writes, another grades against explicit criteria, and the writer revises with the feedback until it passes.

Most production "AI features" are workflows. Many products sold as agents are mostly workflows with an agentic step in the middle. That's a good design, not a compromise.

lessons.title: Plan, execute, replan
lessons.summary: write the plan down, run it step by step with small executors, replan when reality disagrees

sections.html:
A ReAct agent plans implicitly: each step it decides the next action from the whole history. That works for short tasks. On long ones it drifts: it forgets a requirement, repeats work, or wanders into a subtask and never comes back. The fix every serious agent uses is to make the plan explicit.

Plan-and-execute

  1. A planner call writes a numbered plan for the task.
  2. An executor runs one step at a time. Each step is a small, fresh agent that sees only that step and the results of earlier steps, not the whole messy history.
  3. When a step fails, a replanner sees what is done and what went wrong, and writes new steps for the rest of the task.

This is the structure of Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al. 2023), LLMCompiler, LangGraph's plan-and-execute template, and of deep-research agents. The plan is also a user interface: Cursor and Claude Code show a todo list that the agent updates as it works, which lets you see where it is and stop it early if the plan is wrong.

Todo lists are the modern form

Frontier coding agents don't usually run a separate planner. Instead the model has a todo_write tool and is told to keep its plan in it, marking items in_progress and done. The list lives in the context (and survives compaction because it's re-written), keeps the model honest about what is left, and gives the user a progress view. You'll use exactly that in the capstone. The separate planner in this lab makes the mechanics visible.

Replanning is the point

Plans meet reality. The hotel is sold out, the API returns an error, the file isn't where the plan said. A system that can't replan either fails or, worse, pretends the failed step succeeded. Two rules:

  • An executor must report failure plainly (FAILED: Casa Azul is sold out), never improvise a replacement silently.
  • The replanner keeps the completed steps and only rewrites what remains.

One replan recovered from the sold-out hotel. The executor reported FAILED, the replanner kept steps 1 and 2 and wrote a new step 3 for the next-cheapest hotel, and the total came out right. Without the failure signal, a step executor tends to "succeed" with a made-up booking.

Plan-and-execute used 13 model calls against ReAct's 7. Planning isn't free: a planner call, a replanner call, and a small agent per step that has to finish with a summary. Its peak prompt was only modestly smaller (915 versus 1,014 tokens), because here both are dominated by the four tool schemas sent on every call. Planning's context savings grow with task length, since each executor's context stays small while a single ReAct context keeps growing.

So why plan? For a 4-step task, honestly, ReAct is fine and cheaper. Planning pays off when tasks are long enough to drift, when steps can run in parallel (LLMCompiler executes independent steps of the plan concurrently), when a human should review the plan before anything happens, and when progress must be visible. That's why frontier agents keep the plan as a todo list inside one agent rather than adding a separate planner process for every task.

lessons.title: Reflection with a real verifier
lessons.summary: Reflexion, self-critique and why feedback from tests beats asking the model to try again

sections.html:
Agents get better results by trying, checking, and trying again. The research names for this are Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023: the agent writes a verbal reflection on why it failed and keeps it in memory for the next attempt) and Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023: draft, self-critique, revise). The part that matters in practice is less glamorous: where does the signal that something is wrong come from?

Three sources of feedback, in increasing order of value

  1. None (blind retry). "Try again." At temperature 0 the model writes the same answer. At higher temperature it writes a different answer, which is just sampling: you're doing best-of-n without a way to pick the best.
  2. The model's own critique. "Review your answer for mistakes." It helps on some tasks, but models are poor at finding their own errors without new information. Huang et al. (2024, "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet") found that self-correction without external feedback often makes answers worse.
  3. An external verifier. Tests, a compiler, a type checker, a linter, a schema validator, an API that returns an error, a simulator. These produce new information the model didn't have: "parse_duration('1h 30m') returned 3600, expected 5400". That is what makes the next attempt different.

Coding agents are as strong as they are largely because code comes with verifiers. The loop "edit, run the tests, read the failures, edit again" is reflection with ground truth. It's also why RL on code and math works so well (lesson 13): the same verifiers become rewards.

Running model code safely

The verifier here runs code the model wrote. Treat it as untrusted: run it in a separate process with a timeout (an infinite loop must not hang your agent), capture output, and in production add a sandbox (containers, gVisor, Firecracker microVMs, or a remote sandbox service) with no network and no secrets.

3 → 4 → 5 → 7 with feedback, stuck at 3/7 without. Each test failure told the model something specific (an input, the output, the expectation), so each attempt fixed a class of bug. Blind retries had nothing new to work with. Real models at temperature 0 behave the same way, and at higher temperature you'd get variation without direction.

The sandbox checks matter as much as the loop. The run starts by feeding run_tests an infinite loop and a syntax error: one comes back as "timed out after 2 s (infinite loop?)" and the other as "the code did not run: SyntaxError…", both useful observations instead of a hung or crashed agent.

Tests can be wrong, and models can game them. If the tests come from the model too, it can write tests that pass trivially. Agents under pressure have been seen special-casing test inputs or deleting failing tests. RL-trained models do this "reward hacking" too (lesson 13). Keep verifiers outside the agent's write access when you can, and review diffs to test files.

lessons.title: Humans in the loop
lessons.summary: approval policies, asking the user, pausing and resuming from a checkpoint, and surviving a crash without acting twice

sections.html:
An agent that can only run start-to-finish on its own is either toothless (it only reads) or dangerous (it acts without anyone checking). Real agents pause: to ask a question when the task is ambiguous, and to get approval before an action with consequences. Cursor and Claude Code ask before running shell commands outside an allowlist; ChatGPT's agent asks before purchases and sends; Codex has approval modes from "suggest" to "full auto".

An approval policy is code, not a prompt

"Ask before deleting anything" in a system prompt is a request the model may not honor. The policy belongs in the harness, which sees every call before it runs:

calldecision
a read-only tool (list_jobs)allow: run it
a write (cancel_job)ask the human, unless they said "always" for this tool
a destructive call (delete_checkpoints) on exactly one job folder /ckpt/job-7ask
a destructive call on anything else (/ckpt, /ckpt/job-7/../..)deny without bothering the human
ask_user(question)it's a question for the human, not an action
an unknown tooldeny

Note the asymmetry: a policy can deny on its own, but it never auto-approves something destructive. And "deny without asking" matters for usability. Approval prompts that are almost always "yes" train people to click yes without reading, which is how dangerous actions get through. Ask rarely, and only about things worth reading.

Pausing is a state machine

A human may answer in a second or tomorrow. The agent can't block a thread waiting, so the run becomes state that is saved and resumed:

running ──(model asks for approval / a question)──▶ waiting ──(human replies)──▶ running ──▶ … ──▶ done

The state is just data: the messages, the pending calls that need a reply, which tools the user said "always" for, the step count. advance(state) runs until the agent finishes or needs a human, saves the state and returns. respond(state, replies) attaches answers, and the next advance runs the approved calls first. LangGraph's interrupt() and checkpointers, the OpenAI Agents SDK's approval flow, and Temporal-style durable workflows all implement this same machine.

Checkpoints and crashes

Saving state is easy to get subtly wrong:

  • Write atomically. Write to state.json.tmp, then os.replace it over state.json. A crash mid-write then leaves the old checkpoint intact instead of half a file.
  • Save after every side effect. If the process dies after cancelling job-7 but before recording it, the resumed agent will cancel it again. Here that's harmless; for "send the payment", it isn't. Record each result as soon as the action completes, and make actions idempotent where you can (pass an idempotency key, check before acting).

sections.html:
Three pauses, each worth reading. One question (the production job, which the model noticed and asked about) and two batches of approvals. The read was allowed silently, and rm -r /ckpt was refused without asking: the human was never shown a prompt whose right answer is always "no".

The model asked a question instead of guessing. Tagged production but idle is ambiguous, and "cancel the idle jobs" could include it. A good agent surfaces that ambiguity, and the harness makes ask_user a first-class tool so the question becomes a pause, not a guess written into the final answer.

Zero actions repeated after the crash. The process died while executing approved cancellations. Because run_pending saved the checkpoint after each call, the restarted agent saw job-7's cancellation already recorded and only ran what was left. Move the save to after the loop, run again, and watch a cancellation happen twice.

Approvals need context to be meaningful. "Approve delete_checkpoints({'path': '/ckpt/job-121'})?" is clear here. In real systems show the diff, the command, the recipient and the amount, and say why the agent wants it.

lessons.title: Multi-agent systems
lessons.summary: orchestrator and workers like Deep Research; context isolation, parallel subagents, and what it really costs

sections.html:
A multi-agent system is several agent loops whose inputs and outputs are wired together by code or by another agent. The pattern that has proven itself in production is orchestrator-workers: a lead agent breaks the task into independent pieces, hands each to a subagent with a fresh context, and combines their results.

Anthropic's Research feature, OpenAI's and Google's Deep Research, and Claude Code's Task tool (and Cursor's subagents) all work this way. Each subagent starts with an empty history and one question, does its own searching and reading, and returns a short answer. The lead never sees the raw pages.

Why it helps

  • Context isolation. A researcher that reads ten documents on speculative decoding doesn't carry them into the next question. Each context stays small and on-topic, which helps quality (lesson 04's context rot) and cost.
  • Parallelism. Independent subagents run at the same time. Anthropic reported research queries taking minutes instead of hours with parallel subagents and parallel tool calls.
  • Specialization. Each role gets its own short prompt and tools: a researcher with search, a writer with none.

What it costs, honestly

Anthropic's engineering post on their research system reported that agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x. More tokens bought better answers on broad research questions, where breadth matters and the work splits cleanly. Total tokens can also go down (as in this lab) when one agent would otherwise drag every document through every later step. Which one you get depends on the shape of the task, so measure it.

Multi-agent setups are a poor fit when the subtasks depend on each other or need shared context. Coding is the usual example: two agents editing the same code in parallel make conflicting decisions. Cognition's "Don't build multi-agents" (2025) makes that case: every subagent acts on a partial view of the decisions made so far. The common resolution is single-threaded agents for tightly coupled work, and subagents only for read-only, independent exploration ("search the codebase for X and report back").

The multi-agent setup made more model calls (14 versus 10), and each subagent pays for its own system prompt and tools. With longer documents and more cross-topic steps, isolation wins by more; with many subagents that each re-read the same material, or a lead that pulls their full transcripts back, it loses. Anthropic's 15x number comes from subagents doing much more work (more searches, more sources), which was the goal. Measure tokens per useful answer on your own tasks.

Wall time fell from 1.5 s to 0.9 s because the three researchers ran in parallel. The latency win from parallel subagents is real and grows with the number of independent subtasks.

Read the brief for errors a lead can't see. The writer only knows what researchers reported. If one misread a source, nothing downstream can catch it. Production systems add a citation check: a subagent that verifies each claim against its source.

lessons.title: Evaluating agents
lessons.summary: pass@k versus pass^k, grading the trajectory and not just the answer, and reading traces

sections.html:
You can't improve an agent you can't measure, and agents are hard to measure for three reasons: they're stochastic (the same task passes on one run and fails on the next), they're multi-step (a right answer can come from a wrong process), and their failures are diverse (wrong tool, loop, hallucinated result, unsafe action).

Two numbers, two questions

Run each task n times and count c passes.

  • pass@k: the probability that at least one of k attempts passes. The unbiased estimator (Chen et al. 2021, HumanEval) is 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k). It answers "can the agent ever do this?" and fits settings where something can pick the winner (tests, a human, a verifier).
  • pass^k: the probability that all k attempts pass, C(c, k) / C(n, k), from tau-bench (Yao et al. 2024). It answers "does it do it every time?", which is what matters for an agent acting for users: a customer doesn't get to retry the refund.

As k grows they move in opposite directions. An agent at 75% pass@1 can have pass@4 near 100% and pass^4 near 30%. Report the one that matches how the agent is used.

Grade the trajectory

An agent that gets the right answer by emailing your customer list to itself has not passed. Graders check:

  • Outcome: the answer contains the right fact, the tests pass, the database is in the expected state (tau-bench compares the final DB state).
  • Process: no forbidden tools, no actions the user didn't ask for, a step budget, the right approvals requested.
  • Cost: tokens, time, model calls.

Graders can be code (exact checks, preferable when possible), a model with a rubric ("LLM-as-judge", for open-ended output), or humans (for calibration). Benchmarks you will see: SWE-bench Verified (fix real GitHub issues, graded by the repo's tests), tau-bench (customer service with tools and a simulated user), Terminal-Bench, GAIA, BrowseComp, OSWorld.

Read the traces

Aggregate numbers tell you that something fails. Traces tell you why. Log every run as JSONL (messages, tool calls, results, timing, grade) and read twenty failures before changing anything. Observability tools (LangSmith, Braintrust, Phoenix, Weave, OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions) are mostly ways to store and browse these.

lessons.title: Safety and prompt injection
lessons.summary: anything a tool returns can contain instructions; secrets, least privilege and taint tracking enforced in the harness

sections.html:
A model can't reliably tell your instructions from instructions that appear in its input. When an agent reads an email, a web page, a PDF, a GitHub issue or a tool result, any text in it that looks like an instruction might be followed. That is prompt injection (named by Simon Willison in 2022), and it is the defining security problem of agents. It has been demonstrated against browsing agents, coding agents reading repository files, email assistants and MCP tool descriptions.

The lethal trifecta

Willison's framing: an agent is exploitable when it combines

  1. access to private data (your inbox, your code, an API key in its prompt),
  2. exposure to untrusted content (anything someone else wrote), and
  3. a way to send data out (email, HTTP requests, even rendering an image URL).

Remove any one leg and the data-exfiltration attack fails. Meta's "Agents Rule of Two" (2025) says the same thing as a design rule: in one session, an agent should have at most two of untrusted input, sensitive data/systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally. If it needs all three, a human approves.

Defend in the harness

Training makes models more resistant (instruction hierarchies, injection-aware fine-tuning), and detectors catch known patterns, but neither is a guarantee. Measured attack success rates against frontier models are lower than they used to be and still well above zero. The defenses you can rely on are code in the harness:

  • Secrets never leave in tool arguments. Scan every outgoing call for known secret values. Better: don't put secrets in the prompt at all; give the tool the credential, not the model.
  • Least privilege. The email tool can only send to your company's domain; the file tool can't leave the workspace (lesson 14's safe_path); the shell has an allowlist.
  • Taint tracking. Once untrusted content enters the context, the session is tainted: every action with side effects now needs human approval, because the model's intent may no longer be yours. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025) is a more rigorous version that tracks data flow through a restricted interpreter.
  • Show the human the action, not the model's summary of it. "Send to collect@evil.io" is easy to catch; "I'll share the summary as requested" is not.

In labs/11_safety/agent.py, the Guard class:

  1. observe(tool): after an untrusted tool (tool.meta["untrusted"]) runs, the session is tainted.
  2. check(call, tool): block if any secret appears in json.dumps(call.args); block send_email to a domain outside allowed_domains; while tainted, any tool with risk != "read" needs ask_human(call) to say yes.
  3. execute(box): return an execute(call) function for run_agent that checks, then either returns "Blocked by guardrail: <reason>." or runs the tool and observes it, logging every decision.

python labs/11_safety/run.py --solution

Five attacks (two secret exfiltrations, a data leak to a recruiter, a web page with a hidden HTML comment, a destructive "tidy the inbox") and three normal tasks, with and without the guard. The mock model is gullible on purpose: it follows instructions it reads, as models sometimes do.

fields.label: attacks that worked, with the guard

sections.html:
5/5 to 0/5 without touching the model. Each attack was stopped by a different rule: two by the secret scan (one of them to an address inside the allowed domain, "IT" asking to rotate the key, which a domain allowlist alone would have let through), two by the recipient allowlist, and one, "delete all emails matching invoice", by taint tracking: the session had read untrusted content, so the delete needed approval, and the human said no.

The normal tasks still worked, at a price of 3 approvals. Forwarding Bob's notes to Alice after reading an email is legitimately tainted, so it asks. That friction is the cost of safety, and it's why you want the human prompt to show the exact recipient and body. Approving should take one glance.

Why not just tell the model to ignore instructions in emails? Put it in the system prompt and it helps, sometimes. But the attacker writes the text the model reads, and can iterate until it works; your system prompt is fixed. Rules in code don't negotiate.

MCP raises the stakes. Tool descriptions from third-party MCP servers are also untrusted text in the prompt ("tool poisoning"), and a server's tools can change after you approve them. Review the servers you install like dependencies.

lessons.title: The Model Context Protocol
lessons.summary: tools in another process, discovered at runtime over JSON-RPC; build a server that works in Cursor

sections.html:
Until now every tool has been a Python function in the agent's own process. That doesn't scale: every agent (Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT, your own) would need its own integration with every system (GitHub, Jira, Postgres, your cluster). The Model Context Protocol (MCP, Anthropic, late 2024, now supported across the industry) turns N×M integrations into N+M. A system exposes its tools once as an MCP server, and any MCP client can discover and call them.

The protocol

MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 over a transport: stdio for local servers (the client starts the server as a subprocess and they exchange one JSON object per line) or Streamable HTTP for remote ones. A session:

client → {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{...}}}
server ← {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{"tools":{}},"serverInfo":{"name":"gpu-cluster",...}}}
client → {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}            (a notification: no id, no reply)
client → {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}
server ← {"result":{"tools":[{"name":"gpu_inventory","description":"...","inputSchema":{...}}]}}
client → {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"job_status","arguments":{"job_id":"job-121"}}}
server ← {"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"job-121: failed: CUDA out of memory at step 300"}],"isError":false}}

Three details trip people up:

  • Tool failures are results, not protocol errors. An unknown tool or an exception inside a tool returns a normal result with isError: true, so the model sees the message (lesson 02's rule again). JSON-RPC errors such as -32601 Method not found are for protocol problems.
  • stdout is the protocol. A stray print() in a stdio server corrupts the stream. Log to stderr.
  • The tool list is discovered at runtime. The client asks the server what it has, and the server can announce changes (notifications/tools/list_changed). The schemas go into the model's prompt like any other tool.

Besides tools, MCP servers can offer resources (data the client can read into context), prompts (templates), and ask the client for sampling (a model call) or elicitation (a question for the user). Most servers you'll meet only do tools.

In labs/12_mcp/agent.py:

  2. MCPClient: start the server with subprocess.Popen(..., stdin=PIPE, stdout=PIPE, text=True); request writes one JSON line and reads lines until the matching id; notify; initialize; list_tools; call_tool (join the text content, prefix Error: when isError); close.
  3. as_tools(client): wrap each server tool as an agentlab Tool whose function calls client.call_tool. Bind the name per tool: a closure in a loop captures the variable, not its value.

sections.html:
The agent code didn't change. as_tools turned three remote tools into ordinary Tool objects, and run_agent from lesson 02 used them without knowing they lived in another process. That's the point of a protocol: the loop, the context management and the approvals stay the same; only where tools come from changes.

**Two parallel calls became two tools/call requests.** The model asked for the inventory and the job status at once. Over stdio they go one after another on one pipe; a server over HTTP could handle them concurrently.

Errors stayed observations. format_disk (unknown) and gpu_inventory(region="mars") (raises) came back as isError results the model can read, while a protocol-level mistake (tools/destroy) got -32601. Mixing these up is the most common MCP server bug.

Treat MCP servers like dependencies. A server runs with your permissions, and its tool descriptions are text in your model's prompt (lesson 11's tool poisoning). Install servers you trust, pin versions, and prefer servers that ask for approval on writes.

lessons.title: How agentic models are trained and served
lessons.summary: trajectories as SFT data, verifiable rewards and GRPO, and why prefix caching decides what agents cost

sections.html:
You know training and inference. This lesson connects them to everything you've built: why models are good at the loop at all, and what the loop does to a serving system.

Training: from base model to agent

A base model has never seen <tool_call>. Agentic behavior comes from post-training in roughly three stages.

1. SFT on trajectories. Collect agent runs (human-written, or generated by a stronger model and filtered for success), render them with the chat template (lesson 00), and fine-tune. The key detail is the loss mask: the loss is only on tokens the model wrote: its reasoning, its tool calls, and the <|im_end|> that teaches it to stop. System prompts, user turns and tool results are context, not targets. Training on tool results would teach the model to hallucinate tool outputs instead of waiting for them.

2. RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Sample many rollouts per task in a real environment (a repo with tests, a sandbox with tools, a simulated user) and score each one with a program: tests pass, the answer matches, the database is in the right state. DeepSeek-R1 showed how far this goes for reasoning; agentic models (Claude, the o-series and gpt-oss, Kimi K2, Qwen3, GLM) are trained with large-scale RL in tool environments. The reward is where you encode what "good" means, including cost: a penalty per step teaches efficiency.

3. GRPO-style advantages. Group Relative Policy Optimization (DeepSeekMath, 2024) drops PPO's value network. For each task it samples a group of G rollouts and uses the group as the baseline:

Ai = (ri - mean(r)) / (std(r) + ε)

Rollouts better than their siblings get pushed up, and worse ones down. If every rollout gets the same reward (all succeed or all fail), every advantage is zero and the task teaches nothing. That's why curricula keep tasks at the edge of the model's ability.

Reward hacking is the constant enemy: models learn to special-case tests, skip verification, or claim success. Environments need verifiers that can't be gamed, and that's much of the engineering effort in agentic RL.

Serving: the loop meets the KV cache

Each agent step is a new request whose prompt is the previous prompt plus a bit more (lesson 02). Without help the server re-prefills everything every step: O(steps2) prefill compute. Prefix caching fixes this. vLLM's automatic prefix caching hashes KV blocks, and SGLang's RadixAttention keeps a radix tree of cached prefixes. If the new prompt starts with tokens already in the cache, their KV is reused and only the new suffix is prefilled. Providers bill cached input tokens at a steep discount (often 75–90% off) for the same reason.

That puts a constraint on the harness: the prompt must be append-only. Anything that changes an early token invalidates everything after it:

  • a timestamp or random id in the system prompt,
  • tools listed in a different order (a set or dict that isn't ordered deterministically),
  • rewriting old tool results, or compaction (which rewrites the middle, deliberately trading a cache miss for a smaller context).

Claude Code, Codex and Cursor go to some lengths to keep their prefixes stable for exactly this reason.

hit rate, timestamp in the system prompt

sections.html:
Only 17% of a trajectory is training signal. The system prompt with tool schemas, the question and the tool results are 83% of the tokens and carry no loss. The trained spans are just the three assistant turns (two lookups in parallel, the calculator call, the final sentence), each ending in <|im_end|>. Long agent trajectories are expensive to train on per useful token, which is one reason RL (which only needs the reward) scales better than collecting perfect demonstrations.

GRPO ranked the behaviors without a value model. Parallel lookups (+0.80) beat sequential ones (+0.55) only because of the step penalty, and the reward never mentioned parallelism. Mental math scored −1.65, the strongest signal in the group. The dithering-but-correct rollout landed slightly below average (−0.18): right answer, too many steps. Change the step penalty to 0 and parallel and sequential become identical, which is how reward design shapes behavior.

86% of prompt tokens served from cache, append-only. Each request re-uses everything up to the new tool result. Put Current time: 06:00:07 at the start of the system prompt and the hit rate collapses to 0.4%: the first few tokens differ, so nothing after them matches. Rotating the tool order is nearly as bad (3.9%). Rewriting old results lands in between (56%), because the prefix still matches up to the first rewritten message.

Compaction is a deliberate cache miss. Lesson 04 rewrote the middle to keep the context small; this lab shows what that costs at the server. Good harnesses compact rarely and in big steps, so each compaction is followed by many append-only, cache-friendly requests.

lessons.title: Capstone: a coding agent
lessons.summary: a small Claude Code or Cursor agent from the course's parts; exact-match edits, tests as verifier, approvals, todos

sections.html:
Coding agents are the most successful agents so far, and now you can see why: code comes with a verifier (tests), a precise action space (edit this text in this file), and plenty of training environments (lesson 13). Underneath, Claude Code, Cursor's agent, Codex and SWE-agent are the loop from lesson 02 with a carefully designed set of tools.

The tools

toolwhy it looks like this
list_files(), grep(pattern)agentic search: find code by reading, instead of pre-loading the repo into the context (lesson 04)
read_file(path)returns line numbers, so the model and the errors can talk about locations
edit_file(path, old, new)exact-match replace: old must appear exactly once. No line numbers to get wrong, no whole-file rewrites to truncate. Claude Code's Edit and Cursor's StrReplace work this way
run_tests()the verifier (lesson 07): runs in a subprocess with a timeout, output clipped
todo_write(items)the plan as a list the model rewrites as it works (lesson 06), shown to the user

And the harness around them:

  • Path safety. Every path is resolved and must stay inside the repository: ../../etc/passwd, /etc/passwd and symlinks pointing out are refused (lesson 11's least privilege).
  • Helpful edit errors. When old isn't found, the error names the closest line and says to check indentation. When it appears twice, it says how many times and asks for more context (lesson 03).
  • Approvals on writes. Edits ask the human (or are auto-approved in a sandbox); reads never ask (lesson 08).

The classic mistake

read_file shows 10| return s[len(s) // 2]. Models copy that line, line number and all, into edit_file's old, and the edit fails. It's one of the most common coding-agent errors, and the fix is in the tool, not the model: a clear error with the closest real line, which the model can paste back. Real harnesses also strip a leading line-number prefix from old automatically.

sections.html:
Two bugs fixed in 9 model calls, verified by the tests. The agent ran the tests first, so it knew what was wrong before reading code, read the one file the tracebacks pointed to, made two minimal edits, and re-ran the tests before claiming success. Run the tests, read, edit, verify: that order is what you want from any coding agent, and the system prompt asks for it explicitly.

The failed edit cost one model call and one approval. The mock copied the line-number prefix, like real models do, and the error's "Closest line is 10: ' return s[len(s) // 2]'" gave it the exact text. On the second bug it didn't repeat the mistake. Without the hint, models often retry with variations of the wrong string, or fall back to rewriting the whole file.

Everything here came from an earlier lesson. The loop (02), tool design and helpful errors (03), a todo list (06), tests as the verifier (07), approvals (08), path safety (11). coding_agent accepts lesson 04's compact too: for a real repo, plug it in with a budget and clip run_tests output with keep=r"FAIL|ERROR|Error|line \d+".

Next steps for a real one. Add run_shell(cmd) with an allowlist and approvals, checkpoint the state after every edit (lesson 08) so a long session survives a crash, show diffs in approvals, and evaluate it on a few dozen bugs with pass^k (lesson 10). That is, in miniature, how SWE-bench agents are built and measured.

lessons.title: The frontier, mapped to what you built
lessons.summary: how Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Deep Research and computer-use agents are put together, and the frameworks around them

sections.html:
Every frontier agent product is built from the pieces in this course. What distinguishes them is how carefully each piece is engineered, and how the model was trained for that harness. Here is the map.

Coding agents: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Devin, SWE-agent

piecelessonwhat they do
