Cloud and background agents (Codex cloud, Cursor background agents, Devin, Jules) run the same loop in a remote sandbox with a clone of your repo and hand back a pull request. That's lesson 08's resumable state taken to its conclusion: the run is fully detached from your laptop.

Research agents: Deep Research and friends

Orchestrator-workers (lesson 09): a lead plans the research, spawns parallel searchers with fresh contexts, and a writer synthesizes with citations. It runs for many minutes and reads hundreds of sources, so context isolation and compaction aren't optional. The models are RL-trained on browsing tasks with verifiable answers (benchmarks like BrowseComp measure this).

Computer-use and browser agents

The same loop, with screenshots as observations and mouse/keyboard actions as tools (OpenAI's computer-using agent, Anthropic's computer use, Gemini's computer use model). Everything gets harder: observations are large images (context), actions are imprecise (tool design), and the web is full of injected instructions (lesson 11). That is why these products confirm with you before purchases, logins and sends.

Frameworks

You built the core of each of these yourself, so you can read their docs as "where is the loop, where is the state, where are the approvals?":

  • OpenAI Agents SDK: agents, tools, handoffs between agents, guardrails, tracing; runs against any OpenAI-compatible model.
  • Claude Agent SDK: the Claude Code harness as a library: its tools, context management, subagents, hooks and permissions.
  • LangGraph: agents as explicit state graphs with checkpointers and interrupt() for humans in the loop (lesson 08's state machine, generalized).
  • Google ADK: agents, workflow agents (sequential, parallel, loop), multi-agent hierarchies; A2A, a protocol for agents calling other agents.
  • smolagents (Hugging Face): small and readable; "code agents" whose actions are Python snippets rather than JSON tool calls.
  • Pydantic AI, CrewAI, AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework, Mastra (TypeScript): typed tools and outputs, role-based crews, multi-agent conversations.
  • DSPy: programs of LLM calls whose prompts are optimized against a metric rather than hand-written (lesson 10's evals as the training signal).

A rule of thumb: use a framework when you need what it adds (durable state, tracing, a team's shared conventions), and keep the loop simple enough that you could rewrite it in an afternoon. Anthropic's advice from "Building effective agents" still holds: many successful production agents are a few hundred lines of plain code.

What to read next

  • Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (2024); "How we built our multi-agent research system" (2025); "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (2025); "Writing effective tools for agents" (2025).
  • Yao et al., ReAct (2022); Shinn et al., Reflexion (2023); Yang et al., SWE-agent (2024); Yao et al., tau-bench (2024).
  • Simon Willison on prompt injection and the lethal trifecta; Meta, "Agents Rule of Two" (2025); Debenedetti et al., CaMeL (2025).
  • DeepSeekMath (GRPO, 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) for RL with verifiable rewards.
  • The MCP specification at modelcontextprotocol.io.

Your next projects

  1. Run lab 14 against a real model: serve Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (or bigger) with vLLM or SGLang and --model vllm:…, add three new bugs to the toy repo, and measure pass^k over 10 trials.
  2. Put lesson 04's compaction and lesson 08's checkpoints into the coding agent, and make it survive a kill -9 mid-session without repeating an edit.
  3. Turn your cluster tools from lesson 12 into a real MCP server for something you use daily, and use it from Cursor.
  4. Use lesson 13's pieces to generate SFT data from your agent's successful runs, fine-tune a small model on it, and compare its pass@1 before and after.

cards.q: What is an AI agent, mechanically?
cards.a: A program (the harness) that calls a model in a loop: send messages plus tool schemas, run any tool calls the model asks for, append the results, repeat until the model answers without calling tools.

cards.q: What does a chat template do?
cards.a: It renders messages, tool schemas and tool results into the single token sequence the model was trained on, with special tokens marking roles and turn boundaries, and ends with the generation prompt.

cards.q: Where do tool definitions live in the model's input?
cards.a: In the system prompt, as text (JSON schemas inside <tools> for Qwen). They are re-sent and re-read on every request.

cards.q: How does a model "call a tool"?
cards.a: It writes text in a format it was trained to use, e.g. <tool_call>{"name": ..., "arguments": ...}</tool_call>; the server parses that text into structured tool_calls.

cards.q: In ChatML (Qwen 2.5), how do tool results go back to the model?
cards.a: As a user turn containing one <tool_response>…</tool_response> block per result.

cards.q: What is the generation prompt, and why does it matter?
cards.a: The trailing <|im_start|>assistant\n that opens the model's turn. Without it the model may continue the user's text instead of answering.

cards.q: Why does using the model's own chat template matter?
cards.a: The model learned its tool-call and turn conventions in post-training; a different format is out of distribution and degrades tool use noticeably.

cards.q: What three things make up a tool definition the model sees?
cards.a: A name, a natural-language description, and a JSON schema of the parameters (types, descriptions, enums, required list).

cards.q: Why put an enum in a tool schema?
cards.a: It tells the model the exact accepted values (and lets constrained decoding enforce them), eliminating near-miss strings like "h100" or "H100 SXM".

cards.q: What is the most common silent failure when a server can't parse a tool call?
cards.a: The call text is returned as ordinary content, so the harness sees no tool calls and treats it as the final answer: the agent stops without acting.

cards.q: Why must a truncated tool call be reported as an error rather than "no calls"?
cards.a: Otherwise the loop ends on a half-written call; an explicit error lets the harness retry, e.g. with a larger max_tokens.

cards.q: Why is isinstance(True, int) a validation trap?
cards.a: In Python bool is a subclass of int, so a naive check accepts true for an integer parameter. Check bool explicitly first.

cards.q: What is constrained (guided) decoding?
cards.a: The server compiles a JSON schema or grammar into a state machine and masks logits each step so only valid continuations can be sampled; invalid JSON becomes impossible.

cards.q: What does constrained decoding not fix?
cards.a: Semantic errors: a well-formed call with a job id that doesn't exist, or the wrong tool for the task. You still validate and return helpful errors.

cards.q: Write the agent loop in four lines of pseudocode.
cards.a: reply = model(messages, tools); append reply; if no tool calls: return reply.text; else run each call and append its result; repeat (bounded).

cards.q: What does ReAct stand for and what is its key idea?
cards.a: Reason + Act: interleave reasoning, tool actions and observations so each observation informs the next step.

cards.q: Who decides that an agent is finished?
cards.a: The model, by replying without tool calls. The harness only enforces limits (steps, tokens, time, cost).

cards.q: Why must tool errors be returned as results instead of raised?
cards.a: The model can read the error and fix its call; raising crashes the run, and hiding the error leaves the model guessing.

cards.q: Why does an agent's total prompt-token cost grow roughly quadratically with steps?
cards.a: Each step re-sends the full history, which grows linearly with steps; summing over steps gives a quadratic total.

cards.q: What are parallel tool calls, and what do they save?
cards.a: Several independent calls in one model reply; they save a model round trip per call and can execute concurrently.

cards.q: What must be true of tool results in the message history?
cards.a: Every tool call in an assistant message gets exactly one result, matched by tool_call_id, before the next assistant turn.

cards.q: What is the agent-computer interface (ACI)?
cards.a: The tools, their descriptions, inputs, outputs and errors, treated as a user interface designed for a model, from the SWE-agent paper.

cards.q: What should a good tool description contain?
cards.a: What the tool does and returns, when to use it (and when not to), and the expected input formats, with an example if useful.

cards.q: Why is "Did you mean: …" in an error message so effective?
cards.a: It gives the model the exact valid values to retry with, turning a dead end into a one-step recovery.

cards.q: What is poka-yoke in tool design?
cards.a: Designing tools so mistakes are impossible or harmless: enums, coercion of unambiguous types, absolute paths, bounded outputs, safe defaults.

cards.q: When is it right to coerce a model's argument?
cards.a: Only when the intent is unambiguous, like "3" for an integer or "true" for a boolean. Never for anything that changes meaning.

cards.q: Many overlapping tools or a few sharp ones?
cards.a: A few sharp ones: overlapping tools confuse selection and every definition costs prompt tokens on every call.

cards.q: What is context rot?
cards.a: The degradation of a model's recall and reasoning as its context grows, well before the hard limit; facts in the middle of long contexts are used less reliably.

cards.q: What are the three main context-management techniques for agents?
cards.a: Clip tool outputs at the source, compact (summarize) old history when over a budget, and fetch context just in time with tools instead of pre-loading it.

cards.q: How should a tool's long output be clipped?
cards.a: Keep head and tail lines plus every line matching what matters (errors, failures), with explicit markers for elided gaps.

cards.q: What does compaction keep verbatim?
cards.a: The system prompt, the task, and the most recent turns; the middle is replaced by a model-written summary that preserves progress and key facts.

cards.q: Why must compaction never split a tool call from its result?
cards.a: A tool message without its calling assistant message is an invalid history: APIs reject it and models misread it.

cards.q: Why is "drop the oldest messages" bad for agents?
cards.a: The oldest turns hold the task's plan and progress; dropping them makes the agent forget what it did and repeat work or loop.

cards.q: Name two forms of memory that persist beyond one context window.
cards.a: Notes or scratchpad files the agent writes and re-reads (e.g. a todo list or NOTES.md), and long-term memory stores retrieved into the prompt when relevant.

cards.q: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent (Anthropic's definition)?
cards.a: In a workflow your code fixes the sequence of LLM calls; in an agent the model decides its own steps and tool use dynamically.

cards.q: When should you prefer a workflow over an agent?
cards.a: When the steps are known in advance: workflows are cheaper, faster, more predictable and easier to test.

cards.q: What is routing?
cards.a: Classifying an input with one LLM call and dispatching it to a specialized prompt, tool chain or model for that category.

cards.q: Why do threads speed up parallel LLM calls in Python despite the GIL?
cards.a: The calls are I/O-bound (waiting on the network or GPU), and the GIL is released while waiting.

cards.q: What are the two kinds of parallelization in "Building effective agents"?
cards.a: Sectioning (independent subtasks run at once) and voting (the same task run several times and aggregated).

cards.q: What makes an evaluator-optimizer loop converge?
cards.a: A reviewer with explicit criteria that says specifically what is missing, plus a cap on rounds.

cards.q: What are the three roles in plan-and-execute?
cards.a: A planner that writes the steps, an executor that runs each step (often a small fresh agent), and a replanner that rewrites the remaining steps after a failure.

cards.q: Why does a ReAct agent drift on long tasks?
cards.a: Its plan is implicit in a growing history; requirements and progress get buried, so it forgets, repeats or wanders.

cards.q: What must an executor do when a step fails?
cards.a: Report the failure explicitly (e.g. "FAILED: sold out") rather than improvising or claiming success, so the replanner can react.

cards.q: What does a replanner keep, and what does it rewrite?
cards.a: It keeps completed steps and their results and rewrites only the remaining steps.

cards.q: How do modern coding agents keep a plan without a separate planner?
cards.a: With a todo_write tool: the model maintains a todo list in its own context, marking items in_progress and done, which the UI shows to the user.

cards.q: When is plan-and-execute not worth it?
cards.a: On short tasks: it costs extra model calls (planner, replanner, per-step summaries) and its context savings only matter as tasks grow long.

cards.q: What is Reflexion?
cards.a: An agent pattern where after a failed attempt the model writes a verbal reflection on what went wrong, which is kept in context to guide the next attempt.

cards.q: Why does "try again" without feedback rarely help?
cards.a: At temperature 0 the model repeats itself; at higher temperature it only resamples. No new information enters the context.

cards.q: What did "LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet" find?
cards.a: Without external feedback, asking models to review and correct their own reasoning often fails to improve, and can degrade, accuracy.

cards.q: Give four examples of external verifiers for agents.
cards.a: Unit tests, compilers or type checkers, linters, schema validators, API error responses, simulators, or a human reviewer.

cards.q: How should an agent run model-written code?
cards.a: In a separate process with a timeout and captured output, and in production inside a sandbox with no network and no secrets.

cards.q: What is reward hacking in a coding agent?
cards.a: Satisfying the verifier without solving the task, e.g. special-casing test inputs or editing the tests themselves.

cards.q: Where should an agent's approval policy be enforced, and why?
cards.a: In the harness, before each tool call runs; a rule in the prompt is a request the model may ignore, while code always runs.

cards.q: Name the four possible decisions for a tool call in this lab's policy.
cards.a: allow (run now), ask (human approval), deny (block without asking), human (a question for the user via ask_user).

cards.q: Why should a policy deny some calls without asking the human?
cards.a: Prompts whose answer is always "no" waste attention and train people to approve without reading; reserve prompts for real decisions.

cards.q: Why must a human-in-the-loop agent be a resumable state machine?
cards.a: Humans reply after seconds or days; the run must be saved as data (messages, pending calls, settings) and resumed later, possibly in another process.

cards.q: How do you write a checkpoint safely?
cards.a: Write to a temporary file and atomically rename it over the old one (os.replace), so a crash never leaves a partial checkpoint.

cards.q: How do you avoid repeating side effects after a crash?
cards.a: Record each action's result in the checkpoint immediately after it completes, and make actions idempotent where possible.

cards.q: What should an approval prompt show?
cards.a: Exactly what will happen (command, diff, recipient, amount) and why the agent wants to do it.

cards.q: What is the orchestrator-workers pattern?
cards.a: A lead agent decomposes a task into subtasks, delegates each to a worker (subagent) with a fresh context, and synthesizes their results.

cards.q: What is context isolation, and why does it help?
cards.a: Each subagent starts with an empty history and only its subtask, so its context stays small and on-topic, and the lead sees only condensed findings.

cards.q: When are multi-agent systems a poor fit?
cards.a: When subtasks are tightly coupled or need shared decisions, like parallel edits to the same code; agents acting on partial context make conflicting choices.

cards.q: Roughly how many tokens did Anthropic report multi-agent research uses compared with chat?
cards.a: About 15x (single agents about 4x); the extra tokens bought better results on broad research tasks.

cards.q: Why can multi-agent use fewer total tokens than one agent?
cards.a: A single agent re-sends every document it has read on every later step; isolated subagents each re-send only their own.

cards.q: How do frontier coding agents usually use subagents?
cards.a: For read-only, independent exploration (search the codebase, research a question) that returns a short report, while one main agent makes the edits.

cards.q: Define pass@k and its unbiased estimator.
cards.a: The probability at least one of k attempts passes; with n samples and c passes, 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k).

cards.q: Define pass^k. Which benchmark introduced it?
cards.a: The probability that all k attempts pass, C(c, k)/C(n, k); introduced by tau-bench to measure reliability.

cards.q: Why is pass^k the right metric for customer-facing agents?
cards.a: Users can't pick the best of several attempts; the agent must succeed every time, which is what pass^k measures.

cards.q: Why grade the trajectory and not just the final answer?
cards.a: A correct answer can come from forbidden or harmful actions (unrequested emails, deleted data) or an unaffordable number of steps.

cards.q: What are the three kinds of graders?
cards.a: Code-based checks (exact, preferred), model-based rubric graders (LLM-as-judge), and human review (for calibration).

cards.q: What should you log for every agent run?
cards.a: The full trajectory (messages, tool calls with arguments, results), timing, token usage and the grade, as structured data such as JSONL.

cards.q: What does SWE-bench Verified measure?
cards.a: Whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues, graded by running the repository's tests on its patch.

cards.q: What is prompt injection?
cards.a: Instructions embedded in content an agent reads (emails, web pages, files, tool results) that the model follows as if they came from its user or developer.

cards.q: What is the lethal trifecta?
cards.a: Private data access + exposure to untrusted content + an exfiltration channel. An agent with all three can be made to leak data.

cards.q: State Meta's Agents Rule of Two.
cards.a: In one session an agent should have at most two of: untrusted inputs, access to sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally; otherwise require human approval.

cards.q: What is taint tracking in an agent harness?
cards.a: Marking the session once untrusted content enters the context, then requiring approval for every side-effecting action from that point on.

cards.q: Why are harness rules more reliable than "ignore instructions in emails" in the prompt?
cards.a: The attacker controls the injected text and can iterate until the model complies; code checks run on every call regardless of what the model was persuaded to do.

cards.q: Why is "don't put secrets in the prompt" the best secret defense?
cards.a: A secret the model never sees can't be leaked; give credentials to the tool implementation instead.

cards.q: What is MCP tool poisoning?
cards.a: Malicious instructions hidden in a third-party MCP server's tool descriptions, which the model reads as part of its prompt.

cards.q: What problem does MCP solve?
cards.a: It standardizes how agents discover and call external tools, so each system exposes an MCP server once and every MCP client can use it (N+M integrations instead of N×M).

cards.q: What wire format and transports does MCP use?
cards.a: JSON-RPC 2.0, over stdio for local servers (newline-delimited JSON) or Streamable HTTP for remote ones.

cards.q: List the messages of an MCP session that calls one tool.
cards.a: initialize → result; notifications/initialized; tools/list → tools; tools/call → content and isError.

cards.q: How should an MCP server report that a tool raised an exception?
cards.a: As a normal tools/call result with isError: true and the message as text, not as a JSON-RPC error.

cards.q: What does JSON-RPC error -32601 mean?
cards.a: Method not found: the request named a method the server doesn't implement.

cards.q: Why must a stdio MCP server never print to stdout?
cards.a: stdout carries the protocol; any extra output corrupts the JSON stream. Logs go to stderr.

cards.q: Besides tools, what can an MCP server offer?
cards.a: Resources (readable data), prompts (templates), and requests to the client for sampling (a model call) or elicitation (asking the user).

cards.q: In SFT on agent trajectories, which tokens get loss?
cards.a: Only the assistant's own tokens: its reasoning, its tool calls and the end-of-turn token; not system, user or tool-result tokens.

cards.q: Why must tool results be masked out of the SFT loss?
cards.a: Training on them would teach the model to generate (hallucinate) tool outputs itself instead of stopping and waiting for real results.

cards.q: What is RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR)?
cards.a: Reinforcement learning where rollouts are scored by a program (tests pass, answer matches, state is correct) rather than a learned reward model.

cards.q: Write the GRPO advantage.
cards.a: For a group of G rollouts of the same prompt, A_i = (r_i − mean(r)) / (std(r) + ε); the group is the baseline, with no value network.

cards.q: What happens in GRPO when every rollout in a group gets the same reward?
cards.a: All advantages are zero, so the task contributes no gradient. Tasks must be neither always solved nor never solved.

cards.q: What is prefix caching, and why do agents benefit so much?
cards.a: Reusing the KV cache of a prompt prefix already computed; agent steps share almost their whole prompt with the previous step.

cards.q: Name three harness habits that destroy prefix-cache hits.
cards.a: A timestamp or random id early in the prompt, non-deterministic tool ordering, and rewriting earlier messages (including compaction).

cards.q: What is reward hacking in agentic RL?
cards.a: The policy maximizing the reward without doing the task, e.g. special-casing tests or claiming success, exploiting a weak verifier.

cards.q: Why do coding agents use exact-match string replacement for edits?
cards.a: It needs no line numbers that drift, can't truncate a whole-file rewrite, and fails loudly (not found or not unique) instead of editing the wrong place.

cards.q: What should edit_file do when old appears twice?
cards.a: Refuse and say how many matches there are, asking for more surrounding lines so the match is unique.

cards.q: What is the most common edit_file mistake models make, and the fix?
cards.a: Copying read_file's line-number prefix into old; the tool should return the closest real line in its error (or strip the prefix).

cards.q: How does safe_path prevent escaping the workspace?
cards.a: Resolve the joined path (following .. and symlinks) and require that it equals the root or has the root among its parents.

cards.q: Why should a coding agent run the tests before editing?
cards.a: The failures say what is wrong and where; reading code without them is guessing.

cards.q: What makes coding particularly well suited to agents?
cards.a: A cheap, objective verifier (tests and compilers), a precise text action space, and abundant environments for RL training.

cards.q: Name four tools nearly every coding agent has.
cards.a: File read with line numbers, search (grep/glob), exact-match edit, and a shell or test runner; usually also a todo list and web fetch.

cards.q: What is "plan mode" in coding agents?
cards.a: The agent investigates and writes a plan for you to review and approve before it makes any edits.

cards.q: How do cloud/background coding agents differ from local ones?
cards.a: The same loop runs in a remote sandbox with a clone of the repo, detached from your machine, and returns its work as a branch or pull request.

cards.q: What makes computer-use agents harder than tool-calling agents?
cards.a: Observations are large screenshots, actions (clicks, typing) are imprecise, and web content is full of untrusted instructions.

cards.q: Which framework models agents as explicit state graphs with interrupts for humans?
cards.a: LangGraph, with checkpointers and interrupt().

cards.q: What is a smolagents "code agent"?
cards.a: An agent whose actions are Python code snippets executed in a sandbox, instead of JSON tool calls.

cards.q: What does DSPy optimize?
cards.a: The prompts (instructions and few-shot examples) of a multi-step LLM program, against a metric on a dataset.
